title: A Canary in the Neural Mine: Catching an Image Classifier’s Silent, Confident Failures

paper.title: A Canary in the Neural Mine: Catching an Image Classifier’s Silent, Confident Failures
paper.abstract: Abstract Deployed vision models auto-accept confident predictions, so high-confidence errors propagate silently. Maximum Softmax Probability (MSP), the standard failure predictor, has a structural blind spot: as a scalar read from the classifier head, it is first-order blind to feature variation orthogonal to its confidence gradient. Through a factorial analysis of feature-space detectors, we identify a conditional-redundancy principle explaining why they fail to complement MSP: the class-separability geometry they measure is already encoded in MSP and collapses under fusion. The signal that survives is class-conditional typicality on the off-manifold residual—and because this residual’s distribution varies by backbone, from near-Gaussian to heavy-tailed, it must be estimated non-parametrically. We instantiate these findings as CANARY, a training-free detector that computes a per-class kNN distance on the PCA residual of the penultimate feature, percentile-calibrates it on validation data, and fuses it with MSP through a single validation-tuned weight. CANARY’s benefit follows a headroom law: gains grow as baseline MSP quality falls, so a single clean-validation number forecasts the improvement. With every parameter selected on in-distribution data alone, CANARY matches or improves 382 of 385 shift cells (e-AURC; 379 on AUROC) across five backbones, with worst-case regression within seed noise ( − 0.0002 -0.0002 AUROC) and the largest gains on natural distribution shifts (ImageNet-A/R, ObjectNet)—where deployed models are most exposed.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Deployed vision models operate under selective classification: they auto-accept predictions when confident and abstain when uncertain. The safety of this pipeline relies entirely on accurate failure prediction, defined as the model’s ability to rank correct predictions above incorrect ones. When ranking fails at high confidence, errors propagate silently into deployment. Maximum Softmax Probability (MSP) remains the canonical baseline for failure prediction, but it suffers from a structural blind spot. By collapsing the D D -dimensional feature space to a scalar confidence, MSP is first-order insensitive to an entire ( D − 1 ) (D-1) -dimensional hyperplane of feature variation—on ViT-B/16, 767 of 768 dimensions (Section 4.1 ). Feature-space methods such as ViM and the Mahalanobis family exploit exactly this discarded geometry—yet, designed for OOD detection, they consistently underperform MSP when transplanted to failure prediction (Section 2 ). Figure 1 : The Headroom Law across shift families. CANARY’s fusion AUROC gain (y-axis) is inversely related to the backbone’s baseline MSP AUROC on the clean ImageNet-1k validation set (x-axis). This predictable negative-slope relationship holds consistently across both synthetic ((a) ImageNet-C) and natural shifts ((b) ImageNet-A, (c) ImageNet-R), with natural shifts exhibiting the most substantial gains. Dashed line: a same-architecture control (two ViT-B/16 fine-tunes) isolating MSP quality as the driver of the gain (Section 6 ). To understand exactly what information in the feature space complements MSP, we decompose the design space of feature-based failure prediction into a factorial experiment over three axes: projection basis, distance metric, and reference conditioning. This analysis reveals a conditional-redundancy principle: the class-separability geometry that most feature detectors measure is redundant with MSP under fusion—the classifier head has already extracted those directions. What survives fusion is off-manifold typicality, and it imposes two requirements: the score must be non-parametric, because the residual’s distribution varies by backbone, and class-conditional, because global typicality breaks under natural shifts (Section 4 ). We introduce CANARY, a minimal, training-free instantiation of these findings: a per-class kNN distance on the PCA residual of the penultimate feature, percentile-calibrated and fused with MSP through a single validation-tuned weight. Because CANARY isolates precisely the signal MSP lacks, its benefit is predictable: fusion gains grow as baseline MSP quality falls (Figure 1 ), so a single clean-validation number forecasts the gain before deployment—small where MSP is already a near-ceiling ranker, largest on weak backbones and natural shifts. A same-architecture control isolates the driver: two ViT-B/16 fine-tunes differing only in MSP quality show gains of + 0.42 +0.42 vs. + 0.08 +0.08 pp, ruling out architectural confounds. This predictability yields a concrete operational property—empirically, CANARY is never worse than the MSP it augments. Across 385 shift cells on five backbones, it matches or improves 382 cells (e-AURC; 379 AUROC); the exceptions (3 on e-AURC, 6 on AUROC) lie within seed noise (worst case − 0.0002 -0.0002 AUROC). Its gains concentrate on natural, real-world shifts (ImageNet-A, ImageNet-R, ObjectNet) rather than synthetic corruptions. Contributions: • Conditional-Redundancy Principle. A factorial analysis over basis, distance, and conditioning showing that class-separability geometry is redundant with MSP under fusion; the complementary signal is non-parametric, class-conditional, off-manifold typicality (Section 4 ). • Headroom law. Fusion gains decrease predictably with baseline MSP quality, isolated from architecture by a same-architecture control and validated across nine ImageNet backbones (including self-supervised DINOv2), a different label space (CIFAR-100), and a held-out covariate shift (ObjectNet) (Section 6 ). • CANARY. A training-free, post-hoc detector realizing the blueprint; it matches or exceeds MSP on 382 of 385 shift cells with worst-case regression within seed noise, with the largest gains on natural shifts (Sections 5 – 6 ).

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Logit- and Activation-Based Detection. MSP [ 16 ] remains the canonical baseline for failure prediction. Logit-space corrections, such as MaxLogit [ 13 ] , Energy [ 25 ] , Doctor [ 10 ] , and GEN [ 26 ] , rely purely on the information already exposed by the linear classifier head, inherently inheriting MSP’s structural blind spot. Because any score read from the logit vector alone is invariant to feature variation orthogonal to the classifier head, it cannot retroactively distinguish confident errors from correct predictions; extensive evaluations confirm none consistently outperform MSP [ 19 ] . Activation-shaping heuristics ( e.g . , ReAct [ 34 ] , ASH [ 4 ] , DICE [ 35 ] ) modify features before logit computation. However, being calibrated primarily on CNN statistics, they suffer from severe architecture sensitivity. When transplanted to structurally different models like Vision Transformers, their performance often degrades sharply. Feature-Space Detection. To bypass the logit bottleneck, methods like Mahalanobis [ 23 ] , Deep kNN [ 36 ] , ViM [ 39 ] , and Kernel PCA [ 6 ] leverage broader feature geometry. However, these methods were designed specifically for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection. Detecting a confidently misclassified in-distribution sample is structurally distinct from flagging an anomalous OOD input. Consequently, when transplanted to failure prediction, they consistently—and often substantially—underperform the MSP baseline. Furthermore, heuristic parameter-free combinations ( e.g . , ViM adding an energy term, or NNGuide [ 31 ] scaling logits) implicitly assume their constituent tests provide independent signals. As we demonstrate, this assumption fails: class-geometry scores are conditionally redundant with MSP under fusion, meaning a feature-based partner like fDBD [ 24 ] contributes only through its off-manifold component. Closest to our design is SIRC [ 40 , 41 ] , which combines the softmax score with a class-agnostic feature norm (a feature L 1 L_{1} [ 18 ] or ViM residual norm). In contrast, our approach uses a class-conditional off-manifold residual. Prior work has neither isolated the individual contributions of these design choices nor explained their inconsistent outcomes—a gap our factorial analysis addresses (Section 4 ). Failure Prediction and Selective Classification. Dedicated failure predictors like TrustScore [ 20 ] , ConfidNet [ 2 ] , and OpenMix [ 44 ] score misclassifications directly. ConfidNet and OpenMix train auxiliary heads, whereas TrustScore operates post-hoc and ranks predictions by agreement with class-conditional neighbors in feature space. Against this backdrop, none of these predictors isolates the signal that survives fusion with MSP.

sections.heading: 3 Preliminaries
sections.text: Selective Classification. Let f : 𝒳 → ℝ C f:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{C} be a neural network trained to classify inputs x ∈ 𝒳 x\in\mathcal{X} into one of C C classes, with predicted class y ^ = arg ​ max c ⁡ f c ​ ( x ) \hat{y}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{c}f_{c}(x) . In the selective classification framework, the model is equipped with a confidence scoring function s ⁡ ( x ) ∈ ℝ s(x)\in\mathbb{R} and a threshold τ \tau : it outputs the prediction y ^ \hat{y} if s ⁡ ( x ) ≥ τ s(x)\geq\tau , and abstains otherwise. An ideal score ranks all correct predictions above all incorrect ones, so that errors are rejected first as the threshold τ \tau increases. The MSP Baseline and Feature Space. We decompose f f into a feature extractor and a linear classifier head. Let ϕ ⁡ ( x ) ∈ ℝ D \phi(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{D} denote the penultimate feature vector; the logits are z ⁡ ( x ) = W ​ ϕ ​ ( x ) + b z(x)=W\phi(x)+b , with W ∈ ℝ C × D W\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times D} and b ∈ ℝ C b\in\mathbb{R}^{C} the classifier weights and biases. The predicted distribution is p ⁡ ( x ) = Softmax ⁡ ( z ⁡ ( x ) ) p(x)=\mathrm{Softmax}(z(x)) , and Maximum Softmax Probability (MSP), the canonical failure-prediction baseline, defines confidence as the highest class probability, s MSP ​ ( x ) = max c ⁡ p c ​ ( x ) s_{\mathrm{MSP}}(x)=\max_{c}p_{c}(x) . Because s MSP s_{\mathrm{MSP}} is derived solely from the C C -dimensional logit vector z ⁡ ( x ) z(x) , it collapses the D D -dimensional feature geometry—a structural bottleneck we formally analyze in Section 4 . Evaluation Protocol: Isolating Ranking Quality. The Risk–Coverage curve plots selective risk (the error rate on the accepted subset) against coverage as the threshold τ \tau varies; AURC is its integral. Raw AURC is confounded by base accuracy—a more accurate model makes fewer errors and so scores a lower AURC regardless of ranking quality, and the oracle optimum AURC ∗ \mathrm{AURC}^{*} is fixed entirely by the base error rate. To isolate ranking quality we follow the fd-shifts protocol [ 19 ] and adopt the Excess AURC, e-AURC = AURC − AURC ∗ \text{e-AURC}=\mathrm{AURC}-\mathrm{AURC}^{*} [ 9 ] (reported × 10 3 \times 10^{3} ), as our primary metric: zero for a perfect predictor, lower is better, and comparable across backbones of differing accuracy. As secondary, gaming-resistant evidence we report AUGRC [ 38 ] ( P ⁡ ( accept ∩ wrong ) P(\text{accept}\cap\text{wrong}) , which abstaining on easy samples cannot inflate); AUROC serves only as a rank-sanity check.

sections.heading: 4 What Complements MSP? A Factorial Analysis of the Feature Residual
sections.text: To build a detector that complements MSP without degrading baseline performance, we first isolate the exact information discarded by the classifier head, and then measure which of that discarded signal actually survives fusion. Existing feature-space methods entangle several design choices over a chosen feature, specifically the projection subspace (basis), the distance metric, and the reference population (conditioning). This entanglement makes it impossible to attribute their failures to any single factor. We deconstruct this space through a controlled factorial experiment (Figure 2 ). The orthogonal blind spot (Section 4.1 ) and the conditional-redundancy principle (Section 4.2 ) establish exactly why the feature residual is the correct geometric object. Following this, we determine how to evaluate it along the three fundamental axes of distance, basis, and conditioning.

sections.heading: 4.1 The Orthogonal Blind Spot of Linear Heads
sections.text: Every logit-based score factors through z ⁡ ( x ) = W ​ ϕ ​ ( x ) + b z(x)=W\phi(x)+b , and MSP further reduces z z to the scalar φ ⁡ ( z ) = max c ⁡ Softmax ​ ( z ) c \varphi(z)=\max_{c}\mathrm{Softmax}(z)_{c} . By the chain rule, ∇ ϕ s MSP = W ⊤ ​ ∇ z φ \nabla_{\phi}s_{\mathrm{MSP}}=W^{\top}\nabla_{z}\varphi spans a single direction in ℝ D \mathbb{R}^{D} . This scalar collapse leaves MSP first-order blind to the ( D − 1 ) (D-1) -dimensional hyperplane orthogonal to that gradient—on ViT-B/16, 767 of the model’s 768 feature dimensions. Since the gradient direction varies with the input, this statement is local. It therefore supplies only a necessary condition: a complementary signal must vary transverse to MSP’s gradient. Which transverse component actually survives fusion is an empirical question, answered by the factorial analysis (Sections 4.2 – 4.5 ). This limitation persists even when the head has full column rank in feature space (here D = 768 < C = 1000 D{=}768<C{=}1000 , so W W can span all of ℝ D \mathbb{R}^{D} ): a full-rank head guarantees that the logit map discards nothing, but MSP’s scalar collapse of the logits still does.

sections.heading: 4.2 The Conditional-Redundancy Principle
sections.text: Figure 2 : The residual factorial and its fate under fusion. (a) Standalone main effects on the ViT-B/16 penultimate residual (validation AUROC): conditioning strictly dominates ( Δ ​ 5.6 \Delta 5.6 pp), while distance ( Δ ​ 1.5 \Delta 1.5 pp) and basis ( Δ ​ 2.1 \Delta 2.1 pp) are secondary. Marginals exclude the AE to prevent its Mahalanobis degeneracy from inflating the secondary axes. (b) Fused with MSP, this large standalone advantage collapses to ≈ 0.2 \approx 0.2 pp across backbones (conditional redundancy). (c) Per-class conditioning remains essential for robustness: on natural-adversarial ImageNet-A its fused gain stays positive on every backbone while global weakens and reverses (ViT-B/16). Cross-entropy training is expected to concentrate class-discriminative variation in the directions the head reads; if so, a distance computed in the full D D -dimensional space (Mahalanobis [ 23 ] , Deep kNN [ 36 ] ) is dominated by class-separability geometry—precisely what MSP already encodes. Conditioning is by far the dominant standalone axis ( Δ ​ 5.6 \Delta 5.6 pp AUROC; Figure 2 a), dwarfing distance ( Δ ​ 1.5 \Delta 1.5 pp) and basis ( Δ ​ 2.1 \Delta 2.1 pp). But standalone performance is the wrong criterion for a detector deployed in fusion with MSP. Once fused, the conditioning advantage collapses to ≈ 0.2 \approx 0.2 pp on every backbone (Figure 2 b): its variance is shared with MSP, which already encodes the class separability that conditioning exploits. We call this the conditional-redundancy principle: class-geometry signals are redundant with MSP under fusion. A detector escapes redundancy only by projecting away the principal subspace and scoring the residual r ⁡ ( x ) r(x) .

sections.heading: 4.3 Distance: The Necessity of a Non-Parametric Estimator
sections.text: Figure 3 : Residual non-Gaussianity is backbone-dependent. Median per-class excess kurtosis ( x x ) vs. bimodal-class fraction ( y y ), one point per backbone. The kurtosis axis separates the near-Gaussian and heavy-tailed regimes; bimodality does not. Per-class densities in Appendix 0.A . Beyond isolating r ⁡ ( x ) r(x) , the scoring function must accurately reflect the residual’s underlying distribution. Existing methods like ViM and Mahalanobis summarize the residual with parametric quantities (such as an L 2 L_{2} norm or a shared-covariance Gaussian), implicitly assuming a zero-mean, near-isotropic density. The validity of this assumption is strongly backbone-dependent (Figure 3 ; Appendix 0.A ). For instance, the per-class residuals of ViT-B/16 and DINOv2 remain close to Gaussian (median excess kurtosis 0.12 0.12 and 0.24 0.24 ), whereas those of Swin-B and the CNNs are heavily leptokurtic (median 1.0 1.0 – 2.1 2.1 ). Consequently, no single parametric density transfers across these structural regimes. The standard shared-covariance assumption under-fits near-Gaussian residuals by ignoring class-specific variations. Conversely, modeling a full per-class covariance over-fits the heavy-tailed regimes (Swin-B and the CNNs), performing strictly worse than the shared-covariance baseline. The optimal parametric choice fluctuates with the backbone’s geometry, and incorporating mixture components fails to close the performance gap (Appendix 0.B ). A non-parametric kNN estimator sidesteps this dilemma entirely. By measuring the distance to the k k nearest training-set neighbors, it reproduces the best parametric density on the near-Gaussian backbones (within ∼ 0.01 {\sim}0.01 AUROC) and is the single best estimator where tails are heavy. No parametric family is uniformly best, whereas kNN is uniformly near-best.

sections.heading: 4.4 Basis: PCA and the Coordinate Problem
sections.text: Figure 4 : Basis is inconsequential under kNN. Under the deployed per-class kNN estimator, the choice of basis is nearly inconsequential. PCA, AE, and VAE [ 21 ] all perform within a 0.2 0.2 pp margin, with the VAE’s nominal 0.1 0.1 pp advantage falling entirely within crossfit seed noise (Figure 4 ). Because kNN evaluates local geometry directly, it is inherently coordinate-free, making the specific factorization of the residual largely irrelevant. The same holds for a cosine-kernel basis: replacing PCA with the cosine-kernel PCA of [ 6 ] moves CANARY’s fused AUROC by at most 0.0007 0.0007 across four backbones (Appendix 0.J ). We therefore adopt PCA. Training-free, deterministic, and parameter-free, it matches the best performance at zero added computational cost. The single exception is the overcomplete TopK-SAE [ 8 ] , trailing by ∼ 2 {\sim}2 pp. Its dynamic, per-input atom selection projects same-class residuals into varying coordinate systems. This inconsistency dissolves the cohesive per-class clusters that kNN relies on to measure typicality (Appendix 0.C ).

sections.heading: 4.5 Conditioning: Class-Conditional vs. Global Typicality
sections.text: The last axis is the reference population. A global residual score asks whether a feature is atypical of the entire training set, whereas a class-conditional score asks whether it is atypical of its predicted class y ^ \hat{y} . For synthetic, near-isotropic corruptions a global score suffices, but structured natural shifts such as ImageNet-A and ImageNet-R induce class-dependent off-manifold variation, and under fusion the two scores diverge sharply (Figure 2 c). There a global reference, blind to the predicted class, is actively misled exactly where per-class typicality still tracks error. Most of the standalone conditioning gap is redundant with MSP and collapses under fusion (Section 4.2 ), but this robustness residual is not, and it is systematic. Across backbones the per-class residual variance shows a moderate positive correlation with the per-class failure rate (Spearman 0.44 0.44 – 0.64 0.64 ; Appendix 0.D ). An error is best read as a violation of the predicted class’s off-manifold structure, exposing the limits of global atypicality under shift. Summary. Each competing design fails under fusion for its own reason: a full-space distance duplicates MSP, a parametric norm mismodels the residual’s distribution, and a global reference conditions on the wrong population. What survives all three tests—a non-parametric, class-conditional typicality on the orthogonal residual—is the blueprint for the method we detail in Section 5 .

sections.heading: 5 Method
sections.text: Our proposed method, CANARY , is the minimal instantiation of the blueprint distilled in Section 4 , coupling the resulting residual score to MSP through a single validation-tuned weight. Let ϕ ⁡ ( x ) ∈ ℝ D \phi(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{D} denote the penultimate feature of a frozen classifier, and y ^ ​ ( x ) \hat{y}(x) its predicted class. CANARY fits strictly on the ID-correct training samples, 𝒟 ✓ = { ( x i , y i ) ∣ y ^ ​ ( x i ) = y i } \mathcal{D}^{\checkmark}=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\mid\hat{y}(x_{i})=y_{i}\} , to capture the typical geometry of correctly classified features.

sections.heading: 5.1 Low-Rank PCA Residual
sections.text: We compute PCA on the 𝒟 ✓ \mathcal{D}^{\checkmark} features. Let μ ∈ ℝ D \mu\in\mathbb{R}^{D} be the mean and V K ∈ ℝ D × K V_{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times K} the top- K K eigenvectors. The residual is the projection of the centered feature onto the orthogonal complement: r ⁡ ( x ) = ( I − V K ​ V K ⊤ ) ​ ( ϕ ⁡ ( x ) − μ ) . r(x)=\bigl(I-V_{K}V_{K}^{\top}\bigr)\bigl(\phi(x)-\mu\bigr). (1) This projection isolates the feature variation left unexplained by the class-separating directions, the redundant component MSP already captures. We fix K = 512 K=512 . The residual’s K K -dependent variation is precisely that redundant class geometry. Fusion therefore absorbs it, rendering the fused score insensitive to K K on every backbone, even where the residual’s overall gain is large (Appendix 0.E ).

sections.heading: 5.2 Per-Class kNN Distance
sections.text: For each class c c , we group the 𝒟 ✓ \mathcal{D}^{\checkmark} residuals into a reference set ℛ c = { r ( x i ) ∣ ( x i , y i ) ∈ 𝒟 ✓ , y i = c } \mathcal{R}_{c}=\bigl\{r(x_{i})\mid(x_{i},y_{i})\in\mathcal{D}^{\checkmark},\ y_{i}=c\bigr\} . At inference, we score r ⁡ ( x ) r(x) by its Euclidean distance d ( x ) = ∥ r ( x ) − r ( k ) ∥ 2 d(x)=\bigl\lVert r(x)-r^{(k)}\bigr\rVert_{2} to its k k -th nearest neighbor r ( k ) r^{(k)} ( k = 100 k=100 ) in the predicted class’s reference set ℛ y ^ ​ ( x ) \mathcal{R}_{\hat{y}(x)} . These reference sets merely store the training residuals, requiring no covariance fitting or auxiliary training.

sections.heading: 5.3 Percentile Calibration
sections.text: Because the kNN distance d ⁡ ( x ) d(x) is unbounded and backbone-dependent, while MSP operates on an unrelated scale, the two signals must be placed on a common footing prior to fusion. Passing a score through the empirical CDF of its reference distribution performs the probability integral transform, mapping the score to a p p -value that is uniform on [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] for typical inputs. Let 𝒱 \mathcal{V} denote the set of correctly classified validation inputs: s r ( x ) = 1 − F ^ ( d ( x ) ) , F ^ ( t ) = 1 | 𝒱 | ∑ x j ∈ 𝒱 𝟙 [ d ( x j ) ≤ t ] , s_{r}(x)=1-\hat{F}\bigl(d(x)\bigr),\qquad\hat{F}(t)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|}\sum_{x_{j}\in\mathcal{V}}\mathds{1}\bigl[d(x_{j})\leq t\bigr], (2) where 𝟙 ​ [ ⋅ ] \mathds{1}[\cdot] denotes the indicator function (1 if the condition holds, 0 otherwise). A higher s r s_{r} thus marks a more typical, likely-correct input. We calibrate MSP identically against its own validation-correct CDF to obtain s m s_{m} . Both signals are now p p -values computed against a fixed validation reference, reflecting precisely what a deployed system can calculate without access to test labels. These standardized p p -values provide well-calibrated inputs for a Fisher-inspired log-linear combination [ 7 ] .

sections.heading: 5.4 Weighted-Fisher Fusion
sections.text: Percentile calibration yields two p p -values per input: s m ​ ( x ) s_{m}(x) from MSP and s r ​ ( x ) s_{r}(x) from the residual. A Fisher-style combination multiplies the two p p -values (equivalently, sums their logs). We apply a weighted formulation in the logarithmic domain: S ⁡ ( x , w ) = w ​ ln ⁡ s m ​ ( x ) + ( 1 − w ) ​ ln ⁡ s r ​ ( x ) . S(x;\,w)=w\ln s_{m}(x)+(1-w)\ln s_{r}(x). (3) At w = 1 2 w=\tfrac{1}{2} , this recovers the canonical Fisher combination ( s m ​ ( x ) ​ s r ​ ( x ) s_{m}(x)s_{r}(x) ), which assumes equally informative signals. However, our signals are strongly asymmetric. By the conditional-redundancy principle, MSP already captures the residual’s class-relevant signal. Fusion absorbs this redundancy, isolating only the residual’s unique off-manifold component. MSP thus supplies the dominant evidence, prioritized through the validation-tuned weight w w . We tune w w via cross-fitting on the clean validation set. Specifically, we split the set in half, maximizing AUROC on one and evaluating on the other. We repeat this across five random seeds and average the results. Because the fusion relies on a single scalar weight, this low-capacity formulation mitigates over-adaptation to the validation splits. The optimal weight w ⋆ w^{\star} is then frozen for all subsequent shift evaluations. We treat this as a log-linear pooling rule rather than a hypothesis test: since s m s_{m} and s r s_{r} are dependent (Section 4.2 ), we neither invoke nor rely on the test’s independence-based null distribution; w w is tuned empirically and the score is used only for ranking.

sections.heading: 6.1 Setup
sections.text: Datasets. We study failure prediction on ImageNet-1k [ 3 , 33 ] , where the objective is to robustly separate a model’s correct predictions from its own misclassifications under distribution shift. ImageNet-1k validation (50k) serves as the clean, in-distribution reference. We evaluate robustness across three distribution-shift families: ImageNet-C [ 15 ] (15 corruptions × \times 5 severities), ImageNet-A [ 17 ] (natural adversarials), and ImageNet-R [ 14 ] (renditions). ObjectNet [ 1 ] (an independently collected, controlled real-world covariate shift) is held out as a further generalization test. To test transfer to a different label space, we additionally evaluate on CIFAR-100 [ 22 ] and its corrupted variant CIFAR-100-C [ 15 ] . Backbones. To establish architectural generality, we evaluate five main backbones: ViT-B/16 [ 5 ] as the primary architecture, along with ResNet-50 [ 12 ] , Swin-B [ 27 ] , ConvNeXt-B [ 28 ] , and EfficientNet-B4 [ 37 ] . We further probe representational generality using the self-supervised DINOv2 [ 30 ] . To isolate the drivers of CANARY’s gain within a single architecture family, we include three additional ViT configurations: one differently fine-tuned ViT-B/16 that lowers baseline MSP quality while keeping the architecture, size, and pretraining data constant; and two scaled variants (ViT-S/16 and ViT-L/16) that shift MSP headroom through capacity alone, with ViT-L/16 approaching the accuracy ceiling. Finally, the CIFAR-100 experiments employ the standard OpenOOD v1.5 [ 43 ] ResNet-18 and a WideResNet-28-10 [ 42 ] trained with a standard recipe. For every backbone, we fix CANARY’s basis rank K = 512 K{=}512 ( K = D − 128 K=D-128 for the narrower 384-d ViT-S/16 and 512-d CIFAR ResNet-18) and neighbor count k = 100 k{=}100 , and cross-fit the single fusion weight w w strictly on that backbone’s own clean validation split. Full details on the pretrained checkpoints and the per-backbone optimum w ⋆ w^{\star} are provided in Appendix 0.F . Baselines and metrics. CANARY is compared against 19 post-hoc baselines spanning logit-based, activation-shaping, feature-based, and softmax-combination families. The primary metric is e-AURC, the accuracy-corrected excess area under the risk–coverage curve, which ensures fair comparability across backbones of differing base accuracies; AUGRC and AUROC serve as secondary metrics.

sections.heading: 6.3 Generality Across Regimes
sections.text: CIFAR-100: the never-worse property transfers to a different label space. We evaluate CANARY on CIFAR-100 to test whether its never-worse property holds in a genuinely different label space (100 classes, disjoint from ImageNet). To this end, we use two CIFAR-native models (the standard OpenOOD v1.5 ResNet-18 and a WideResNet-28-10 trained with a standard recipe) that are entirely independent of ImageNet on both the data and pretraining axes. CANARY stays at or above MSP on 136 of 150 cells across the two backbones, with the 14 exceptions on WRN-28-10 all falling within a − 0.0004 -0.0004 AUROC margin that represents effective ties rather than true losses. The mean gains are small because both are CNN backbones whose off-manifold residual is nearly uninformative (standalone residual AUROC ≈ 0.55 \approx 0.55 – 0.57 0.57 vs. ≈ 0.75 \approx 0.75 on ViT features). Consequently, the fusion weight sits at the MSP anchor ( w ⋆ = 0.9 w^{\star}=0.9 – 0.95 0.95 ), consistent with the headroom law. While the boundary-based detector fDBD achieves a higher shift-mean on these cleanly separated features, it lacks the never-worse property across the ImageNet backbones, dropping by up to 0.066 AUROC relative to MSP (Table 2 ). We further vary model capacity along the ViT hierarchy, specifically evaluating ViT-S/16 and ViT-L/16, the smaller and larger siblings of the primary ViT-B/16. sections.heading: 6.4 Computational Cost
sections.text: CANARY adds negligible overhead to existing MSP pipelines. Fitting is training- and backpropagation-free: given the extracted features, building the PCA basis and per-class reference set requires ≈ \approx 1.9 TFLOP, and the resulting reference set occupies just ≈ \approx 0.6 GB for ImageNet-1k on ViT-B/16. At inference, a 768 → \to 256 projection and a single L 2 L_{2} distance add merely ≈ \approx 1.3 MFLOP per query. On an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4080, this translates to an overhead of ≈ \approx 50 μ \mu s per unbatched query, averaging under 2 μ \mu s batched.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: This work elucidates the mechanisms governing MSP-complementary failure prediction: the conditional-redundancy principle shows that the class-relevant geometry of a frozen feature space is absorbed by MSP under fusion, so only the orthogonal, off-manifold component contributes novel information. CANARY operationalizes this principle, measuring class-conditional non-parametric typicality on the PCA residual and fusing it with MSP via a single validation-tuned weight. Evaluated under a strictly deployment-realistic protocol without retraining or OOD data exposure, CANARY delivers its largest gains where MSP is weakest, closely following the headroom law, while degrading gracefully toward MSP where the baseline is already strong. Crucially, it remains empirically never-worse, not regressing meaningfully below the baseline MSP across hundreds of distribution shifts, diverse backbone architectures, and even a different label space. Limitations. We identify two primary limitations. First, while our findings are robustly validated across diverse shift sets and backbones and grounded in a geometric rationale, they remain empirical. We have yet to provide a rigorous mathematical formalization regarding the joint distribution of the fused scores. The headroom law, in particular, is an empirical regularity established over the nine backbones and shift families studied here rather than an analytical derivation, and its exact functional form may differ beyond this regime. Second, CANARY is structurally blind to purely on-manifold confident failures, where a shifted input is genuinely typical of an incorrect class and leaves no off-manifold trace. However, this represents only a subset of hard natural shifts. On ImageNet-A, for instance, CANARY still improves upon MSP because many challenging samples retain an off-manifold component; only the strictly on-manifold remainder lies beyond its reach. Future work. Subsequent research should aim to formalize the conditions under which the empirical never-worse property holds, and to derive an analytical bound for the headroom law, currently established as an empirical forecast. Methodologically, closing the on-manifold gap requires integrating external signals ( e.g . , boundary-distance or raw-input heuristics). Fusing these with CANARY’s off-manifold typicality offers a promising path toward comprehensive failure prediction without surrendering its never-worse reliability. Finally, expanding CANARY to dense prediction tasks ( e.g . , per-pixel typicality), adversarial settings, and high-stakes domains ( e.g . , medical imaging) remains an important direction. sections.heading: Appendix 0.C Why the TopK SAE basis underperforms
sections.text: Section 4.4 evaluates the choice of basis under the deployed per-class kNN estimator. This section provides a finer geometric perspective underlying those results. The SAE residual does not occupy a fixed subspace. Instead, its overcomplete code selects a different set of active neurons per input. Consequently, same-class residuals lack a shared coordinate system, loosening the per-class clusters that kNN relies on. Because the code is trained strictly to reconstruct, its leftover is dominated by hard-to-reconstruct, instance-specific details. Empirically, reconstruction quality and failure-prediction performance do not align. PCA at a bottleneck of K = 256 K=256 leaves 27.8% of the feature variance unexplained (0.2775). The overcomplete TopK SAE (latent dimension 6144, sparsity 32) leaves a smaller 26.2% (0.2623) unexplained. However, under the per-class kNN, the SAE yields an AUROC of 0.7264, falling strictly behind PCA’s 0.7662—a ∼ 4 {\sim}4 pp gap at this reconstruction-matched K = 256 K=256 ; against the deployed K = 512 K=512 PCA (AUROC 0.747) the SAE still trails by the ∼ 2 {\sim}2 pp quoted in Section 4.4 . A smaller reconstruction residual thus does not buy a better failure-prediction score. This confirms that the cause is fundamentally geometric rather than a matter of residual size. Any fixed basis recovers the off-manifold geometry equally well, making PCA the natural, training-free choice. Figure 6 : The SAE underperformance is geometric. On ViT-B/16, despite reconstructing slightly better than PCA, the overcomplete TopK SAE scores worse under the per-class kNN.

sections.heading: Appendix 0.D Per-Class Residual Variance Predicts Failure
sections.text: The advantage of the per-class conditioning discussed in Section 4.5 is systematic. Specifically, a class whose in-distribution (ID) correct residuals are more dispersed is inherently more failure-prone. For each class c c , we measure the per-class residual total variance over its ID-correct training residuals: tr ⁡ ( Σ c ) = 1 | 𝒞 c | ​ ∑ i ∈ 𝒞 c ∥ r i − μ c ∥ 2 , \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_{c})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_{c}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}_{c}}\lVert r_{i}-\mu_{c}\rVert^{2}, (4) where 𝒞 c \mathcal{C}_{c} is the set of ID-correct training samples for class c c , and μ c \mu_{c} is their residual mean. Alongside this, we calculate the per-class validation failure rate, defined as fail c = 1 − acc ⁡ ( val ∣ true class ​ c ) \mathrm{fail}_{c}=1-\mathrm{acc}(\text{val}\mid\text{true class }c) . We then compute the Spearman rank correlation between the residual variances { tr ⁡ ( Σ c ) } \{\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_{c})\} and the failure rates { fail c } \{\mathrm{fail}_{c}\} across all 1,000 classes for each backbone. Backbone Spearman ρ \rho (Variance vs. Failure) ViT-B/16 0.55 ConvNeXt-B 0.64 Swin-B 0.61 ResNet-50 0.49 EfficientNet-B4 0.61 DINOv2 0.44 The correlation is consistently positive and moderate on every backbone, ranging from 0.44 to 0.64. Consequently, the per-class residual spread systematically tracks where errors are most likely to occur. A global reference inherently discards this crucial class-specific failure information by pooling all classes into a single distribution.

sections.heading: Appendix 0.E Robustness to the Basis Rank K K
sections.text: CANARY is K K -insensitive across backbones. Sweeping K K at matched fractions of the feature dimension D D and evaluating across all shift families, the fused AUROC of CANARY varies by at most 0.0021 0.0021 over K / D ∈ [ 0 , 0.9 ] K/D\in[0,0.9] —even on the 2048-d ResNet-50, where K = 512 K=512 leaves the bottom three-quarters of the spectrum as the residual (Figure 7 a). This is not a vanishing-gain artifact: on the large-gain Swin-B (Section 6.2 ), the score moves by under 0.001 0.001 across K ∈ { 0 , … , 512 } K\in\{0,\ldots,512\} . Figure 7 : Robustness to the PCA basis rank K K . (a) On the five main backbones, the CANARY score is robust to the PCA rank K K (varying by ≤ 0.0021 \leq 0.0021 ). (b) A global ViM-style residual norm is strongly K K -dependent. The y y -axis is the mean AUROC over the full 77 shift cells. Why fusion absorbs the K K -dependence. A small K K retains the class-mean directions in the residual—the class-separating axes the classifier head reads, and thus already encoded by MSP (Section 4.2 ). Conditioned on MSP, these carry no additional information, so fusion discards them regardless of K K . This robustness is specific to CANARY’s per-class position statistic: a global ViM-style norm depends on the subspace dimension and swings by 0.014 0.014 – 0.151 0.151 across the same backbones (Figure 7 b). We fix K = 512 K=512 at no performance cost. Because the projection is orthogonal, the trailing ( D − K ) (D{-}K) -dimensional residual preserves the full- D D distances, so the reference set is stored and searched in that reduced space (256-d for ViT-B). Narrower backbones ( D ≤ 512 D\leq 512 ) instead set K = D − 128 K=D-128 , retaining a minimal 128-d residual (ViT-S/16, CIFAR ResNet-18).

sections.heading: Appendix 0.J Comparison with Kernel PCA
sections.text: Kernel PCA (KPCA) [ 6 ] detects out-of-distribution inputs by measuring the reconstruction error of features projected onto a non-linear principal subspace. To compare it with CANARY, we evaluate KPCA in three distinct roles: as a standalone failure detector, fused with MSP, and as an alternative basis for CANARY’s residual. These evaluations span four diverse backbones: ViT-B/16, ResNet-50, Swin-B, and the self-supervised DINOv2. Following the original method, we implement its two explicit-feature-map kernels—cosine (CoP; ϕ ⁡ ( z ) = z / ∥ z ∥ \phi(z)=z/\lVert z\rVert ) and cosine-Gaussian (CoRP; using random Fourier features with M = 4096 M{=}4096 ). We fit PCA on the correctly classified in-distribution validation features, retaining components that explain 90 % 90\% of the variance, and score each input by its reconstruction error. All reported results represent the mean AUROC across 77 shift cells, under the same out-of-sample protocol used in our main experiments. KPCA as a failure detector. On its own, KPCA reconstruction error provides a weak failure signal ( 0.68 0.68 – 0.75 0.75 AUROC), falling well below the MSP baseline (Table 19 ). When fused with MSP using CANARY’s percentile calibration and weighted-Fisher formulation, KPCA regresses below MSP in 6 of 8 cases (by up to 0.027 0.027 AUROC) and only marginally exceeds it in two (CoP on Swin-B and DINOv2, by at most 0.0035 0.0035 ). Furthermore, once fused, the non-linear CoRP kernel consistently trails CoP across all backbones. In contrast, CANARY improves upon MSP across all four backbones, with DINOv2 being the sole instance where CoP + + MSP attains a slightly higher mean than CANARY ( 0.8553 0.8553 vs. 0.8538 0.8538 ). Since both methods share an identical fusion rule, this discrepancy isolates the quality of the underlying signal: a class-agnostic, whole-feature reconstruction error is largely redundant with MSP (Section 4.2 ). Affiliation: Yonsei University, Seoul 03722, Republic of Korea E-mail {wonseok.shin,songkuk}@yonsei.ac.kr Abstract Deployed vision models auto-accept confident predictions, so high-confidence errors propagate silently. Maximum Softmax Probability (MSP), the standard failure predictor, has a structural blind spot: as a scalar read from the classifier head, it is first-order blind to feature variation orthogonal to its confidence gradient. Through a factorial analysis of feature-space detectors, we identify a conditional-redundancy principle explaining why they fail to complement MSP: the class-separability geometry they measure is already encoded in MSP and collapses under fusion. The signal that survives is class-conditional typicality on the off-manifold residual—and because this residual’s distribution varies by backbone, from near-Gaussian to heavy-tailed, it must be estimated non-parametrically. We instantiate these findings as CANARY, a training-free detector that computes a per-class kNN distance on the PCA residual of the penultimate feature, percentile-calibrates it on validation data, and fuses it with MSP through a single validation-tuned weight. CANARY’s benefit follows a headroom law: gains grow as baseline MSP quality falls, so a single clean-validation number forecasts the improvement. With every parameter selected on in-distribution data alone, CANARY matches or improves 382 of 385 shift cells (e-AURC; 379 on AUROC) across five backbones, with worst-case regression within seed noise ( − 0.0002 -0.0002 AUROC) and the largest gains on natural distribution shifts (ImageNet-A/R, ObjectNet)—where deployed models are most exposed. Keywords: Image classification Failure prediction Selective classification Distribution shift 1 Introduction Deployed vision models operate under selective classification: they auto-accept predictions when confident and abstain when uncertain. The safety of this pipeline relies entirely on accurate failure prediction, defined as the model’s ability to rank correct predictions above incorrect ones. When ranking fails at high confidence, errors propagate silently into deployment. Maximum Softmax Probability (MSP) remains the canonical baseline for failure prediction, but it suffers from a structural blind spot. By collapsing the D D -dimensional feature space to a scalar confidence, MSP is first-order insensitive to an entire ( D − 1 ) (D-1) -dimensional hyperplane of feature variation—on ViT-B/16, 767 of 768 dimensions (Section 4.1 ). Feature-space methods such as ViM and the Mahalanobis family exploit exactly this discarded geometry—yet, designed for OOD detection, they consistently underperform MSP when transplanted to failure prediction (Section 2 ). Figure 1 : The Headroom Law across shift families. CANARY’s fusion AUROC gain (y-axis) is inversely related to the backbone’s baseline MSP AUROC on the clean ImageNet-1k validation set (x-axis). This predictable negative-slope relationship holds consistently across both synthetic ((a) ImageNet-C) and natural shifts ((b) ImageNet-A, (c) ImageNet-R), with natural shifts exhibiting the most substantial gains. Dashed line: a same-architecture control (two ViT-B/16 fine-tunes) isolating MSP quality as the driver of the gain (Section 6 ). To understand exactly what information in the feature space complements MSP, we decompose the design space of feature-based failure prediction into a factorial experiment over three axes: projection basis, distance metric, and reference conditioning. This analysis reveals a conditional-redundancy principle: the class-separability geometry that most feature detectors measure is redundant with MSP under fusion—the classifier head has already extracted those directions. What survives fusion is off-manifold typicality, and it imposes two requirements: the score must be non-parametric, because the residual’s distribution varies by backbone, and class-conditional, because global typicality breaks under natural shifts (Section 4 ). We introduce CANARY, a minimal, training-free instantiation of these findings: a per-class kNN distance on the PCA residual of the penultimate feature, percentile-calibrated and fused with MSP through a single validation-tuned weight. Because CANARY isolates precisely the signal MSP lacks, its benefit is predictable: fusion gains grow as baseline MSP quality falls (Figure 1 ), so a single clean-validation number forecasts the gain before deployment—small where MSP is already a near-ceiling ranker, largest on weak backbones and natural shifts. A same-architecture control isolates the driver: two ViT-B/16 fine-tunes differing only in MSP quality show gains of + 0.42 +0.42 vs. + 0.08 +0.08 pp, ruling out architectural confounds. This predictability yields a concrete operational property—empirically, CANARY is never worse than the MSP it augments. Across 385 shift cells on five backbones, it matches or improves 382 cells (e-AURC; 379 AUROC); the exceptions (3 on e-AURC, 6 on AUROC) lie within seed noise (worst case − 0.0002 -0.0002 AUROC). Its gains concentrate on natural, real-world shifts (ImageNet-A, ImageNet-R, ObjectNet) rather than synthetic corruptions. Contributions: • Conditional-Redundancy Principle. A factorial analysis over basis, distance, and conditioning showing that class-separability geometry is redundant with MSP under fusion; the complementary signal is non-parametric, class-conditional, off-manifold typicality (Section 4 ). • Headroom law. Fusion gains decrease predictably with baseline MSP quality, isolated from architecture by a same-architecture control and validated across nine ImageNet backbones (including self-supervised DINOv2), a different label space (CIFAR-100), and a held-out covariate shift (ObjectNet) (Section 6 ). • CANARY. A training-free, post-hoc detector realizing the blueprint; it matches or exceeds MSP on 382 of 385 shift cells with worst-case regression within seed noise, with the largest gains on natural shifts (Sections 5 – 6 ). 2 Related Work Logit- and Activation-Based Detection. MSP [ 16 ] remains the canonical baseline for failure prediction. Logit-space corrections, such as MaxLogit [ 13 ] , Energy [ 25 ] , Doctor [ 10 ] , and GEN [ 26 ] , rely purely on the information already exposed by the linear classifier head, inherently inheriting MSP’s structural blind spot. Because any score read from the logit vector alone is invariant to feature variation orthogonal to the classifier head, it cannot retroactively distinguish confident errors from correct predictions; extensive evaluations confirm none consistently outperform MSP [ 19 ] . Activation-shaping heuristics ( e.g . , ReAct [ 34 ] , ASH [ 4 ] , DICE [ 35 ] ) modify features before logit computation. However, being calibrated primarily on CNN statistics, they suffer from severe architecture sensitivity. When transplanted to structurally different models like Vision Transformers, their performance often degrades sharply. Feature-Space Detection. To bypass the logit bottleneck, methods like Mahalanobis [ 23 ] , Deep kNN [ 36 ] , ViM [ 39 ] , and Kernel PCA [ 6 ] leverage broader feature geometry. However, these methods were designed specifically for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection. Detecting a confidently misclassified in-distribution sample is structurally distinct from flagging an anomalous OOD input. Consequently, when transplanted to failure prediction, they consistently—and often substantially—underperform the MSP baseline. Furthermore, heuristic parameter-free combinations ( e.g . , ViM adding an energy term, or NNGuide [ 31 ] scaling logits) implicitly assume their constituent tests provide independent signals. As we demonstrate, this assumption fails: class-geometry scores are conditionally redundant with MSP under fusion, meaning a feature-based partner like fDBD [ 24 ] contributes only through its off-manifold component. Closest to our design is SIRC [ 40 , 41 ] , which combines the softmax score with a class-agnostic feature norm (a feature L 1 L_{1} [ 18 ] or ViM residual norm). In contrast, our approach uses a class-conditional off-manifold residual. Prior work has neither isolated the individual contributions of these design choices nor explained their inconsistent outcomes—a gap our factorial analysis addresses (Section 4 ). Failure Prediction and Selective Classification. Dedicated failure predictors like TrustScore [ 20 ] , ConfidNet [ 2 ] , and OpenMix [ 44 ] score misclassifications directly. ConfidNet and OpenMix train auxiliary heads, whereas TrustScore operates post-hoc and ranks predictions by agreement with class-conditional neighbors in feature space. Against this backdrop, none of these predictors isolates the signal that survives fusion with MSP. 3 Preliminaries Selective Classification. Let f : 𝒳 → ℝ C f:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{C} be a neural network trained to classify inputs x ∈ 𝒳 x\in\mathcal{X} into one of C C classes, with predicted class y ^ = arg ​ max c ⁡ f c ​ ( x ) \hat{y}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{c}f_{c}(x) . In the selective classification framework, the model is equipped with a confidence scoring function s ⁡ ( x ) ∈ ℝ s(x)\in\mathbb{R} and a threshold τ \tau : it outputs the prediction y ^ \hat{y} if s ⁡ ( x ) ≥ τ s(x)\geq\tau , and abstains otherwise. An ideal score ranks all correct predictions above all incorrect ones, so that errors are rejected first as the threshold τ \tau increases. The MSP Baseline and Feature Space. We decompose f f into a feature extractor and a linear classifier head. Let ϕ ⁡ ( x ) ∈ ℝ D \phi(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{D} denote the penultimate feature vector; the logits are z ⁡ ( x ) = W ​ ϕ ​ ( x ) + b z(x)=W\phi(x)+b , with W ∈ ℝ C × D W\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times D} and b ∈ ℝ C b\in\mathbb{R}^{C} the classifier weights and biases. The predicted distribution is p ⁡ ( x ) = Softmax ⁡ ( z ⁡ ( x ) ) p(x)=\mathrm{Softmax}(z(x)) , and Maximum Softmax Probability (MSP), the canonical failure-prediction baseline, defines confidence as the highest class probability, s MSP ​ ( x ) = max c ⁡ p c ​ ( x ) s_{\mathrm{MSP}}(x)=\max_{c}p_{c}(x) . Because s MSP s_{\mathrm{MSP}} is derived solely from the C C -dimensional logit vector z ⁡ ( x ) z(x) , it collapses the D D -dimensional feature geometry—a structural bottleneck we formally analyze in Section 4 . Evaluation Protocol: Isolating Ranking Quality. The Risk–Coverage curve plots selective risk (the error rate on the accepted subset) against coverage as the threshold τ \tau varies; AURC is its integral. Raw AURC is confounded by base accuracy—a more accurate model makes fewer errors and so scores a lower AURC regardless of ranking quality, and the oracle optimum AURC ∗ \mathrm{AURC}^{*} is fixed entirely by the base error rate. To isolate ranking quality we follow the fd-shifts protocol [ 19 ] and adopt the Excess AURC, e-AURC = AURC − AURC ∗ \text{e-AURC}=\mathrm{AURC}-\mathrm{AURC}^{*} [ 9 ] (reported × 10 3 \times 10^{3} ), as our primary metric: zero for a perfect predictor, lower is better, and comparable across backbones of differing accuracy. As secondary, gaming-resistant evidence we report AUGRC [ 38 ] ( P ⁡ ( accept ∩ wrong ) P(\text{accept}\cap\text{wrong}) , which abstaining on easy samples cannot inflate); AUROC serves only as a rank-sanity check. 4 What Complements MSP? A Factorial Analysis of the Feature Residual To build a detector that complements MSP without degrading baseline performance, we first isolate the exact information discarded by the classifier head, and then measure which of that discarded signal actually survives fusion. Existing feature-space methods entangle several design choices over a chosen feature, specifically the projection subspace (basis), the distance metric, and the reference population (conditioning). This entanglement makes it impossible to attribute their failures to any single factor. We deconstruct this space through a controlled factorial experiment (Figure 2 ). The orthogonal blind spot (Section 4.1 ) and the conditional-redundancy principle (Section 4.2 ) establish exactly why the feature residual is the correct geometric object. Following this, we determine how to evaluate it along the three fundamental axes of distance, basis, and conditioning. 4.1 The Orthogonal Blind Spot of Linear Heads Every logit-based score factors through z ⁡ ( x ) = W ​ ϕ ​ ( x ) + b z(x)=W\phi(x)+b , and MSP further reduces z z to the scalar φ ⁡ ( z ) = max c ⁡ Softmax ​ ( z ) c \varphi(z)=\max_{c}\mathrm{Softmax}(z)_{c} . Which transverse component actually survives fusion is an empirical question, answered by the factorial analysis (Sections 4.2 – 4.5 ). Per-class densities in Appendix 0.A . Beyond isolating r ⁡ ( x ) r(x) , the scoring function must accurately reflect the residual’s underlying distribution. Existing methods like ViM and Mahalanobis summarize the residual with parametric quantities (such as an L 2 L_{2} norm or a shared-covariance Gaussian), implicitly assuming a zero-mean, near-isotropic density. The validity of this assumption is strongly backbone-dependent (Figure 3 ; Appendix 0.A ). For instance, the per-class residuals of ViT-B/16 and DINOv2 remain close to Gaussian (median excess kurtosis 0.12 0.12 and 0.24 0.24 ), whereas those of Swin-B and the CNNs are heavily leptokurtic (median 1.0 1.0 – 2.1 2.1 ). Consequently, no single parametric density transfers across these structural regimes. The standard shared-covariance assumption under-fits near-Gaussian residuals by ignoring class-specific variations. Conversely, modeling a full per-class covariance over-fits the heavy-tailed regimes (Swin-B and the CNNs), performing strictly worse than the shared-covariance baseline. The optimal parametric choice fluctuates with the backbone’s geometry, and incorporating mixture components fails to close the performance gap (Appendix 0.B ). A non-parametric kNN estimator sidesteps this dilemma entirely. By measuring the distance to the k k nearest training-set neighbors, it reproduces the best parametric density on the near-Gaussian backbones (within ∼ 0.01 {\sim}0.01 AUROC) and is the single best estimator where tails are heavy. No parametric family is uniformly best, whereas kNN is uniformly near-best. 4.4 Basis: PCA and the Coordinate Problem Figure 4 : Basis is inconsequential under kNN. Under the deployed per-class kNN estimator, the choice of basis is nearly inconsequential. PCA, AE, and VAE [ 21 ] all perform within a 0.2 0.2 pp margin, with the VAE’s nominal 0.1 0.1 pp advantage falling entirely within crossfit seed noise (Figure 4 ). Because kNN evaluates local geometry directly, it is inherently coordinate-free, making the specific factorization of the residual largely irrelevant. The same holds for a cosine-kernel basis: replacing PCA with the cosine-kernel PCA of [ 6 ] moves CANARY’s fused AUROC by at most 0.0007 0.0007 across four backbones (Appendix 0.J ). We therefore adopt PCA. Training-free, deterministic, and parameter-free, it matches the best performance at zero added computational cost. The single exception is the overcomplete TopK-SAE [ 8 ] , trailing by ∼ 2 {\sim}2 pp. Its dynamic, per-input atom selection projects same-class residuals into varying coordinate systems. This inconsistency dissolves the cohesive per-class clusters that kNN relies on to measure typicality (Appendix 0.C ). 4.5 Conditioning: Class-Conditional vs. Global Typicality The last axis is the reference population. A global residual score asks whether a feature is atypical of the entire training set, whereas a class-conditional score asks whether it is atypical of its predicted class y ^ \hat{y} . For synthetic, near-isotropic corruptions a global score suffices, but structured natural shifts such as ImageNet-A and ImageNet-R induce class-dependent off-manifold variation, and under fusion the two scores diverge sharply (Figure 2 c). There a global reference, blind to the predicted class, is actively misled exactly where per-class typicality still tracks error. Most of the standalone conditioning gap is redundant with MSP and collapses under fusion (Section 4.2 ), but this robustness residual is not, and it is systematic. Across backbones the per-class residual variance shows a moderate positive correlation with the per-class failure rate (Spearman 0.44 0.44 – 0.64 0.64 ; Appendix 0.D ). An error is best read as a violation of the predicted class’s off-manifold structure, exposing the limits of global atypicality under shift. Summary. Each competing design fails under fusion for its own reason: a full-space distance duplicates MSP, a parametric norm mismodels the residual’s distribution, and a global reference conditions on the wrong population. On an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4080, this translates to an overhead of ≈ \approx 50 μ \mu s per unbatched query, averaging under 2 μ \mu s batched. 7 Conclusion This work elucidates the mechanisms governing MSP-complementary failure prediction: the conditional-redundancy principle shows that the class-relevant geometry of a frozen feature space is absorbed by MSP under fusion, so only the orthogonal, off-manifold component contributes novel information. CANARY operationalizes this principle, measuring class-conditional non-parametric typicality on the PCA residual and fusing it with MSP via a single validation-tuned weight. Evaluated under a strictly deployment-realistic protocol without retraining or OOD data exposure, CANARY delivers its largest gains where MSP is weakest, closely following the headroom law, while degrading gracefully toward MSP where the baseline is already strong. First, while our findings are robustly validated across diverse shift sets and backbones and grounded in a geometric rationale, they remain empirical. We have yet to provide a rigorous mathematical formalization regarding the joint distribution of the fused scores. The headroom law, in particular, is an empirical regularity established over the nine backbones and shift families studied here rather than an analytical derivation, and its exact functional form may differ beyond this regime.
